# Trading in the Green Sea

%% Speculative ideas generated by AI at user request; not canon. %%

This is the working trade model accompanying [[Taelgar Climatic Model]]. The intended pattern is **regular, recognizable sailing seasons without equally convenient travel throughout the year**. Merchants can plan around the winds, while onset, storms, cargo availability, and local hazards still make individual voyages uncertain.

The preferred arrangements are a normal same-year **Tollen–Ursk round trip**, a less common option to winter in Ursk, and a longer circuit with **Ursk and Irrla as alternative summer branches**. Dates below are proposed seasonal windows, not established historical departure dates or a compulsory itinerary for every ship.

This remains development material. It does not rewrite the source notes, settle every political or commercial question in the older emails, or turn provisional cargo lists into canon.

## Direct Tollen–Ursk trade

### The usual same-year voyage

| Period | Typical activity | Conditions needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| April–early May | Assemble cargo, arrange purchases, prepare ships or a convoy. | Preparation can precede the northern ports' opening. |
| Mid- to late May | Depart Tollen eastward through the [[Straits of Cymea]]. | Useful northern westerly opportunities persist through the late spring. |
| June | Arrive at Zakat or another authorized Ursk port. | Principal southern ports are usually accessible by late May or early June. |
| June–July | Sell, buy, load, and negotiate within the permitted trading area. | A substantial share of ordinary cargo is already stocked or arranged. Every voyage need not wait for a new expedition into the interior. |
| Mid-July–early August | Depart directly westward for Tollen. | Recurring E–NE winds provide the normal return season. |
| August–early September | Reach home and distribute cargo. | The return fits within the useful summer window, with some allowance for delays. |

An illustrative schedule is **20 May departure → 20 June arrival → 20 July return departure → 20 August home**. These dates express the intended rhythm, not a new dated event. Roughly **three to five weeks per passage** is a planning allowance under favorable conditions; farther destinations such as Praznitsky need additional margin. Convoy performance and precise port-to-port distances remain unassigned.

The eastward northern current assists the outward journey and opposes the summer return. Favorable westward winds must therefore provide useful progress despite that current; the calendar cannot assume both wind and water reverse together. Until current speeds are established, the model should avoid making the northern branch so fast and unbroken that ordinary westbound sailing becomes impractical.

The direct route need not hug an inhospitable coast or call at intermediate northern harbors. This helps preserve the established scarcity of accessible ports west of Ursk. An offshore crossing can still be a familiar, regularly repeated commercial passage.

### A secondary winter in Ursk

A deliberate overwintering voyage can leave Tollen in **September**, reach Ursk in **late September or October**, remain through the winter, and return west in the following **July–August** window. It uses the autumn eastbound season and avoids requiring a winter return. Earlier autumn departures leave a better margin against storms and freeze-up.

This is useful for an unusual commission, a long negotiation, a cargo not available during a short summer visit, or a merchant with reasons to spend more time at the trading port. It is less attractive for ordinary voyages because it ties up ship, crew, and capital. Provisioning, lodging, repairs, and permission for foreigners to remain through winter are necessary **proposed port arrangements**, not details already established by the canonical notes.

A ship can also winter after damage or a missed return window. Missing the preferred season raises the cost and uncertainty of a westward passage; it does not make every later departure physically impossible or automatically imprison every late merchant until the following summer. Exact late-season alternatives remain local decisions.

This preserves the desired distinction: **overwintering is available and intelligible, but neither necessary nor the most common arrangement**.

## The long circuit with two alternative branches

The annual circuit is a characteristic pattern for suitable long-distance ships, especially halfling family ships. It visits a selected set of markets rather than every major port. The two normal branches visit **Ursk or Irrla** during summer; visiting both is an optional extension with a greater time cost.

| Period | Shared route or activity | Ursk branch | Irrla branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Late March–April | Leave Medju westward as southern easterlies become useful. | A late-March or very early-April departure gives the longer route through Cymea a better margin. | Timing is more forgiving, although a long southern trading season still consumes the summer. |
| April–May | Trade at the [[~Maritime Trade Peninsula~\|Maritime Trade Peninsula]] and, if desired, Cymea. | Either continue west to Cymea, or turn north sooner from the peninsula. | Turn toward southeastern Irrla; a Cymean extension is possible but not required. |
| May–June | Use the offshore northbound window. | Aim for Ursk in June or early July, before the summer reversal becomes a persistent obstacle. | Reach the southeastern trading coast in June–July. |
| Summer | Trade and wait for the next useful season. | Business in the permitted Ursk trading ports. | Business around the [[Republic of Svolhas]]. Exact rainfall, ports, and commercial arrangements remain flexible. |
| Mid-September–early October | Begin the eastward autumn passage. | Depart Ursk as northern westerlies return. | Usually depart in late September or early October, after the high retreats south of the trading coast. |
| October–November | Trade through selected central or southern [[Eastern Isles]]. | Both branches can join an itinerary including the [[Vermillion Isles]] / [[Wahacha]] and [[Quanyi]]. | The same selected island sequence can serve this branch. |
| December | Arrive at Medju. | Arrival before the most persistent calms is the normal goal. | The same. |
| January–March | Trade, maintain ships, make arrangements, and prepare to depart. | A southern winter base completes the annual rhythm. | The same. |

The route from the peninsula to Ursk passes west of Irrla with a prudent offshore margin; it does not imply that Irrla's northwestern coastal waters are safe. Routes to Svolhas go around the island's southern side. Exact passages and the locations of seasonal hazards remain to be developed.

The two branches create different commercial choices. Ursk offers the northern goods and connections already established in play; Irrla offers a southeastern island trading season without requiring the longer journey to the northern ports. Neither branch is inherently the default for every halfling family.

### Completing the eastern and southern legs

For a December Medju arrival, autumn navigation needs a **sequence** of opportunities: eastward from Ursk or southeastern Irrla, southward through the selected island markets, and southwestward or westward toward Medju. The retreating high can support this sequence around different parts of its circulation. The warm southern westward current is potentially helpful on the final leg; it does not eliminate light-wind delays near Medju.

The established Wave Dancer connection gives **Praznitsky → Wahacha → Quanyi → Medju** a useful basis. The map locates the Wahacha stop only within its archipelago, not on an invented exact island. This is a central/southern Eastern Isles itinerary, not a traversal of the entire roughly 2,000-mile island chain described in [[Eastern Green Sea]].

Local magical weather, shifting channels, and island-specific seasons can complicate otherwise familiar sailing windows. The working interpretation is that experienced mariners can still recognize the large seasonal pattern. It should not require the magical islands to become uniformly predictable or safe.

An early or fast ship might reach Medju in late November. **December remains the ordinary target**, not a sign that the voyage has already failed. A late-October departure followed by long island stays could push arrival into January, when calms are more troublesome. Shorter trading stops, waiting for a suitable weather interval, or spending a longer season at an island port are plausible responses. Not every voyage must close a circuit in twelve months.

## Passage-budget check

The map protocol assigns **24 statute miles face-to-face to each small hex** in [[Protocol for Regional Maps]]. The following ranges are coarse route measurements from the world map, allowing for different destinations and broad detours. They are not surveyed sailing distances or measurements of every small channel.

Use **60 statute miles per passage day** as a working planning assumption, with **40 miles per day** as a slower sensitivity check. These are assumptions for this model, not established merchant-fleet speeds. A passage day can include sailing through the night where conditions and crewing permit it. Port business and an explicit reserve are added separately; favorable currents are not added again as a second speed bonus.

### From Medju to Ursk

| Route | Approximate distance | Passage days at 60 miles/day | Trading and reserve allowance | Approximate total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Medju → peninsula → Ursk | 2,200–2,600 miles | 37–44 | Four weeks trading + two weeks reserve | 80–90 days |
| Medju → peninsula → Cymea → Ursk | 3,000–3,400 miles | 50–57 | Four weeks trading + two weeks reserve | 90–100 days |

At the central assumption, an early-April departure reaches Ursk around late June on the shorter route, or around early July via Cymea. Leaving in late March gives the Cymean extension a safer margin. The trading allowance is for the southern stops collectively, not four weeks at every port.

At 40 miles per day, these totals grow to approximately **97–107 days** and **117–127 days**, respectively. The longer route then runs into the less favorable late-July or August northbound conditions. The useful adjustment is to depart earlier, shorten the southern trading season, or turn north at the peninsula. The annual circuit is plausible under the central assumptions but should not be promised to every slow vessel following every detour.

### From Ursk or Irrla through the islands to Medju

| Leg | Approximate distance | Passage days at 60 miles/day |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Southeastern Irrla → Vermillion Isles | 1,200–1,500 miles | 20–25 |
| Ursk trading coast → Vermillion Isles | 1,400–1,800 miles | 23–30 |
| Vermillion Isles → Quanyi → Medju | 1,200–1,600 miles | 20–27 |

Adding **three to four weeks of island trading and two weeks of reserve** gives roughly **11–14 weeks** from departure to Medju, depending on branch and stops. A mid-September or early-October departure therefore fits a December arrival; the longest combinations can extend into early January. The whole schedule has less slack if ships wait until late October to leave.

The [[Emerald Song]] provides a useful fast-ship benchmark of approximately 100 miles per day in its own account, not a default for ordinary Green Sea merchants. Likewise, Wellby's recorded late-September–October travel measures only the portion of an existing voyage experienced in play. Neither example removes the need for realistic port time and weather allowances.

## Overlapping regional trade networks

The circular route links shorter networks; it should not imply that most merchants sail around the entire sea.

| Network | Working connections | Consequences |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Western Gulf | Tollen, Sembaran and Tyrwinghan ports, western Cymean connections | More frequent local voyages through much of the year, interrupted by storms and local conditions. These are not all governed by the long circuit's annual calendar. |
| Western Green Sea | Direct Tollen–Ursk trade, Cymea, and connections toward the Maritime Trade Peninsula and/or Irrla | A family of shorter triangles or “diamonds,” with different endpoints and directions. The direct northern voyage remains prominent; intermediate calls are optional. |
| Eastern Green Sea | Peninsula, Irrla, Medju, and selected Eastern Isles | Substantial regional trade with its own markets, rather than an economy dependent entirely on western demand. Exact short-circuit orders and reciprocal seasons remain open. |

Ursk can consequently be much more familiar to Tollenders than Medju or the Eastern Isles. Tollender merchants repeatedly visit the same authorized northern ports. Goods from the farther east more often pass through halfling ships, peninsula merchants, Irrlan intermediaries, or Cymean markets before reaching Tollen. Familiar goods need not produce detailed knowledge of their ultimate origin.

The older [[Email - Green Sea Trade Routes]] contrasts organized Tollender finance and commercial arrangements with halfling family ships' greater freedom to change plans or extend a stay. That distinction suits the calendars: an ordinary Tollender voyage benefits from returning home within one trading season, while a halfling ship may accept a longer circuit. It remains a working commercial contrast, not a rule about every human or halfling merchant. Cargo lists and the precise roles of peninsula and Irrlan merchants need separate development.

## Historical comparison: Indian Ocean seasons

Historical Indian Ocean commerce offers the desired combination of repeatable sailing seasons, waiting in ports, and many overlapping routes. In broad terms, winter northeasterlies favored travel toward East Africa from Arabia and India, while the summer wind regime supported northward return voyages along East Africa and onward across the northern ocean. Usable windows varied by coast and destination; the strongest monsoon could hinder navigation, and a voyage farther south required its own timetable. These were connected regional systems rather than one universal annual loop. [Beaujard, *The Worlds of the Indian Ocean*, navigation and monsoon discussion](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108341004.002).

Merchant correspondence in the [Princeton Geniza Lab's Indian Ocean documents](https://genizalab.princeton.edu/projects/indian-ocean-documents-cairo-geniza) illustrates the people and arrangements behind those connections: partners, cargoes, payments, delays, and extended absences. For Taelgar, the useful inspiration is a port economy organized around arrivals, departures, stored goods, and relationships that outlast one voyage. It does not require copying historical ship designs or making every merchant spend a winter abroad.

## Remaining decisions

- **Port-level geography:** exact Cymean and peninsula stops, a mapped Svolhas approach, and the channels used among the Eastern Isles. The map deliberately gives broad corridors rather than new canonical ports.
- **Performance and reliability:** ordinary vessel speeds, convoy delays, current strengths, and how much seasonal variation merchants normally accept.
- **Overwintering arrangements:** permission, accommodation, provisioning, and repair facilities inside Ursk's restricted foreign trading areas.
- **Regional circuits:** the practical directions and calendars of the shorter western and eastern “diamonds.” The network concept is adopted; every reciprocal leg is not yet assigned a favorable season.
- **Commercial detail:** cargoes, fairs, credit, agents, warehousing, and how the annual pulse differs among Tollender, halfling, peninsula, and Irrlan merchants.

The physical changes required by this calendar are recorded in [[Taelgar Climatic Model#Climatic requirements for navigation|the climate model]]. The principal remaining uncertainty is the reliability and local expression of the selected circulation, rather than the need to force every ship onto one itinerary.
